name: plot3d
description: A 3D math plot in orbit-camera perspective: a wireframe surface z = f(x, y) (NOT a filled/shaded surface — a hand-sketched grid of lines, like a wire mesh model), a parametric space curve (x(t), y(t), z(t)) such as a helix, or a handful of labeled points in 3-space. Choose this scene for ANY request about a 3D surface, saddle, bowl, wireframe, mesh, parametric curve, helix, spiral in 3D, or plotting points in three dimensions — and for what a parameter does to a surface (z = a·x² − b·y² turning from bowl to saddle, a ripple's wavelength, a bump's width). azimuth_deg and elevation_deg are NUMERIC and ANIMATE smoothly — this is the marquee move for this template: animate azimuth_deg by 90-150 to orbit smoothly around the plot ("walk around it"), e.g. {"animate": {"azimuth_deg": 155}, "duration": 3}. The vertical axis is z (the function's/curve's third coordinate); x and y are the other two — this matches ordinary math notation, even though internally the plot orbits around a world y-up axis. Any name in the surface or curve other than x, y (t for a curve) and pi/e is a PARAMETER: give each a value (and min/max for a slider) in `params` and the equation is written above the plot with the current values in place, each value its own part (eq_param_<name>); animate one ({"animate": {"params.a.value": -1}}) and the surface follows. With parameters the z scale is fixed over every value their ranges allow, so a change reads as a change of height. Paused, the viewer ORBITS by dragging the plot, zooms with ctrl/⌘-wheel or a pinch, and changes the parameters by scrubbing or typing the equation's numbers (controls "equation", the default) or on a drawn panel of sliders ("panel"); an explore beat naming nothing invites exactly this. Numbers for text: {plot3d.<name>} per parameter, {plot3d.z_min}, {plot3d.z_max}, {plot3d.mark_0_z}.

surface.description: f(x, y) expression, e.g. "x^2 - y^2" for a saddle, or "a*x^2 - b*y^2" with parameters. Operators + - * / ^, juxtaposition (2x); functions sin cos tan exp ln log10 sqrt abs pow min max; constants pi, e. Sampled on a grid_n x grid_n grid over domain x,y and drawn as row/column wireframe polylines. z is auto-scaled from the sampled min/max so ANY expression (however large its range) fits the plot — you never need to pre-scale it yourself.

t_max.description: default 2*PI (~6.283). For a helix over several turns use a larger multiple of PI, e.g. 12*PI ~= 37.7.

curve.description: A parametric space curve (x(t), y(t), z(t)), e.g. a helix: { x_expr: "cos(t)", y_expr: "sin(t)", z_expr: "t/6", t_max: 37.7 }. Coordinates are NOT auto-scaled (unlike surface) — pick expressions that stay in a reasonable range, roughly single digits.

points.description: A handful of labeled points in 3-space, each drawn as a small sphere.

domain.description: [min, max] world-unit range for both x and y of a surface (default [-1, 1]). Does not affect curve/points.

grid_n.description: Surface grid resolution per axis, 2-20 (default 12) — 12 gives 12 row + 12 column wireframe polylines.

azimuth_deg.description: Camera orbit angle in degrees (default 35). Numeric and ANIMATES — the marquee move: animate this to orbit around the plot.

elevation_deg.description: Camera tilt in degrees (default 22). Numeric and animates.

distance.description: Camera distance override in world units. Usually leave unset — the camera auto-frames whatever is plotted.

zoom.description: Magnification about the plot's centre (default 1, 0.4-3). Numeric and animates.

axis_labels.description: Override the default "x"/"y"/"z" axis label text.

params.description: Parameter name → a number (its value), or {value, min, max, step, label, fixed, control}. min+max give a slider and bound scrubbing and dragging; step defaults to a fiftieth of the range; label names it in the panel ("amplitude a"); fixed: true shows it but the viewer cannot change it; control "box" makes its panel control a number box.

editable.description: Only these parameters may be changed by the viewer (default: all but fixed ones).

controls.description: Where the viewer changes them: the equation's own numbers (default), a panel of sliders/boxes right of the plot, or both.

panel.description: The parameters in the panel, in order (default: the editable ones).

show_equation.description: Write the equation above the plot (default: when it has parameters).

z_range.description: With parameters: the z values the plot's height is scaled to (default: every value the parameters' ranges allow).

at.description: [x, y] on the surface — a number or a parameter's name.

marks.description: Dots ON the surface at (x, y, f(x, y)) — the saddle point, a peak. label true writes the height.

element_ids.axes: SET — the three axes and their letters in one id, e.g. draw [axes]
element_ids.surface: SET — every wireframe line of the surface in one id, e.g. draw [surface]; present when a surface is drawn
element_ids.axis_x / axis_y / axis_z: the three coordinate axes (arrows from the origin), with axis_x_label / axis_y_label / axis_z_label alongside their tips
element_ids.wire_row_<i> / wire_col_<i>: the surface's row/column wireframe polylines (i = 0…grid_n-1), present when a surface is drawn
element_ids.curve: the parametric curve's single polyline, present when a curve is drawn
element_ids.pt_<i> / pt_label_<i>: a point's marker sphere and its label (label present only when given) — ONLY when there is no surface and no curve; one of the three is drawn, surface first, then curve, then points
element_ids.mark_<i> / mark_label_<i>: a mark's dot on the surface (marks[i]) and its label
element_ids.eq: the equation's written line, without its parameter values (they come with it when drawn)
element_ids.eq_param_<name>: a parameter's number in the equation (eq_param_<name>_2 where it appears again) — point, highlight or focus it when the voice names it
element_ids.slider_<name>: panel: a parameter's slider track (its name, value and knob come with it)
element_ids.title: the figure title, when set

examples.request: Show the saddle surface z = x squared minus y squared in 3D.
How do a and b turn a bowl into a saddle?
What does the width σ do to a bell-shaped bump?
Plot the points A and B in 3D.
